title: The Ancient Olympic Games
body: Held at Olympia in honour of Zeus, the Games are traditionally dated from 776 BC and took place every four years for more than a millennium. Only freeborn Greek men could compete, in events such as running, wrestling, boxing and chariot racing, and a sacred truce let athletes and spectators travel safely. The festival faded under the Christian Roman Empire and is usually said to have ended in the late 4th or 5th century AD.

title: Althea Gibson Breaks Tennis's Colour Barrier
body: In 1956 Althea Gibson won the French Championships, becoming the first Black player to win a Grand Slam singles title. She went on to win Wimbledon and the US Nationals in both 1957 and 1958, at a time when tennis was a largely white sport played in exclusive clubs. She later also became the first African American woman to play on the professional golf tour.

title: The First Asian Games
body: The first Asian Games were held in New Delhi in 1951 with athletes from eleven nations. Promoted by the Indian sports official Guru Dutt Sondhi, they aimed to foster friendship among newly independent Asian countries. Held every four years since, they grew into a major multi-sport event.

title: The Arabian Roots of the Thoroughbred
body: Thoroughbred racehorses trace their male lines to three stallions imported into England between about 1680 and 1730: the Byerley Turk, the Darley Arabian and the Godolphin Arabian. Crossed with English mares, they produced a horse bred for speed, and the General Stud Book, begun in the 1790s, recorded the breed's pedigrees. Racing's obsession with bloodlines made the Thoroughbred one of the earliest closely documented animal breeds.

title: Juan Manuel Fangio
body: The Argentine driver Juan Manuel Fangio won the Formula One World Championship five times in the 1950s, driving for four different manufacturers. He raced in an era when crashes were often fatal and safety equipment was minimal. His titles made him a national hero in Argentina and a byword for excellence in motor racing.

title: The Qatar World Cup
body: In 2022 Qatar hosted the first FIFA World Cup in the Middle East and the Arab world. Because of the summer heat it was moved to November and December, interrupting club seasons around the world. The tournament drew intense scrutiny over the treatment of the migrant workers who built its stadiums and infrastructure, and over how it had been awarded.

title: Jesse Owens in Berlin
body: At the 1936 Berlin Olympics, which the Nazi regime used to showcase its ideology, the African American athlete Jesse Owens won four gold medals, in the 100 m, 200 m, long jump and 4 x 100 m relay. His victories undercut claims of 'Aryan' superiority before a global audience. Yet on returning home he still faced segregation and received little official recognition.

title: Ice Hockey Moves Indoors
body: The first recorded organised indoor game of ice hockey was played at the Victoria Skating Rink in Montreal on 3 March 1875, arranged by James Creighton. The players used a flat wooden disc instead of a ball so that it would stay on the ice. Montreal students and club players then drew up rules that spread the sport across Canada and later the world.

title: Ping-Pong Diplomacy
body: In 1971, at the world table tennis championships in Japan, the Chinese team invited the US team to visit China, a gesture approved at the highest levels. The American players' visit was the first by an official American group since the Communist victory in 1949. The exchange helped pave the way for President Nixon's visit to China in 1972.

title: The Birth of Lawn Tennis
body: Tennis grew out of real tennis, an indoor court game played by French and English royalty since the Middle Ages. In 1874 the British army officer Walter Clopton Wingfield patented an outdoor version for lawns, and in 1877 the All England Club held the first Wimbledon Championships. Lawn tennis quickly became popular with both men and women of the Victorian middle classes.

title: Cameroon at the 1990 World Cup
body: At the 1990 World Cup in Italy, Cameroon beat the holders Argentina in the opening match and went on to become the first African team to reach the quarter-finals. The 38-year-old striker Roger Milla, who scored four goals, celebrated each with a dance by the corner flag. Their run helped persuade FIFA to give Africa more World Cup places from 1994.

title: The Queensberry Rules
body: Published in 1867 under the patronage of the Marquess of Queensberry, these rules were drafted by the Welsh sportsman John Graham Chambers. They required padded gloves, three-minute rounds with one-minute rests and a ten-second count for a knockout, replacing the bare-knuckle prize ring. They became the basis of modern boxing.

title: Title IX and Women's Sport
body: Title IX, a 1972 US federal law, banned sex discrimination in education programmes receiving federal funds. Applied to school and university athletics, it obliged institutions to offer women far more sporting opportunities, scholarships and resources. Participation by girls and women rose dramatically, creating the base for American success in women's sport.

title: Australian Rules Football
body: Australian rules football was codified in Melbourne in 1859 by members of the Melbourne Football Club, including the cricketer Tom Wills. It was devised partly to keep cricketers fit in winter and was played on cricket grounds, which explains its large oval fields. Some have suggested a link with marngrook, an Aboriginal ball game, but historians debate this influence.

title: When Kings Banned Football
body: Medieval 'mob football' pitted whole villages or parishes against each other, with few rules and frequent injuries. Rulers repeatedly tried to suppress it: a 1314 proclamation in the name of Edward II banned it in London, and 15th-century Scottish kings outlawed football and golf, partly because they distracted men from archery practice. Some traditional mass games, such as Shrovetide football, still survive in English towns.

title: India's Golden Age of Hockey
body: India won the Olympic field hockey gold medal at every Games from 1928 to 1956, six in a row. The forward Dhyan Chand, famed for his ball control, starred in the victories of 1928, 1932 and 1936. Hockey gave colonial and newly independent India a source of national pride on the world stage.

title: The Rituals of Sumo
body: Sumo has roots in Shinto ritual and was performed at shrines and the imperial court for centuries before professional tournaments developed in the Edo period. Wrestlers throw salt to purify the ring, which is overseen by a referee dressed like a Shinto priest. The highest rank, yokozuna, is named after the thick rope belt these champions wear in ceremonies.

title: Mandela and the 1995 Rugby World Cup
body: In 1995 the newly democratic South Africa hosted and won the Rugby World Cup, beating New Zealand in the final in Johannesburg. Rugby had long been associated with white Afrikaner identity, but President Nelson Mandela wore a Springbok jersey to present the trophy to the captain, François Pienaar. The moment became a symbol of national reconciliation, though how far it changed the sport itself is debated.

title: The Supersuit Era in Swimming
body: In 2008 and 2009 swimmers wearing new polyurethane bodysuits broke world records at an extraordinary rate, as the suits improved buoyancy and reduced drag. Critics called it 'technological doping'. The international swimming federation banned such suits from 2010, limiting their materials and coverage, and the episode became a reference point in debates over technology and fairness in sport.

title: Maradona and the Hand of God
body: In the 1986 World Cup quarter-final in Mexico City, Argentina's Diego Maradona scored against England with his hand, later attributing the goal to 'the hand of God'. Minutes later he dribbled past several England players to score a goal often called one of the finest ever. Coming four years after the Falklands War, the match carried strong political feeling, and Argentina went on to win the tournament.

title: Polo, the Game of Kings
body: Polo originated in Persia, probably well over 2,000 years ago, as training for cavalry, and became a favourite of Persian, Indian and Chinese courts. Under Shah Abbas I, the great square of Isfahan, laid out around 1600, served as a polo ground watched from the royal palace. British officers learned the game in Manipur in north-east India in the mid-19th century and spread its modern form worldwide.

title: Emil Zátopek's Olympic Triple
body: At the 1952 Helsinki Olympics the Czechoslovak runner Emil Zátopek won the 5,000 m, the 10,000 m and, in his first ever race at the distance, the marathon. His punishing interval training influenced generations of distance runners. After supporting the Prague Spring in 1968 he lost his army post and was demoted to manual work.

title: The Mesoamerican Ballgame
body: For more than 3,000 years peoples of Mesoamerica, including the Olmecs, Maya and Aztecs, played a team game with a heavy solid rubber ball, usually struck with the hips. Many stone courts survive, often shaped like a capital I, some with stone rings set high in the walls. The game had religious and political meaning and was sometimes linked to human sacrifice; a version called ulama is still played in parts of Mexico.

title: Cathy Freeman at Sydney 2000
body: At the 2000 Sydney Olympics the Aboriginal athlete Cathy Freeman lit the Olympic cauldron at the opening ceremony and later won the 400 metres. Her victory came amid national debate about reconciliation with Indigenous Australians. She had earlier drawn both criticism and admiration for carrying the Aboriginal flag alongside the Australian flag on victory laps.

title: Kanō Jigorō and Judo
body: In 1882 Kanō Jigorō founded the Kodokan in Tokyo to teach judo, 'the gentle way', a systematised and safer form of jujutsu designed as physical and moral education. Its throws and holds could be practised at full strength without serious injury. Kanō became the first Asian member of the International Olympic Committee, and judo joined the Olympics at Tokyo in 1964.

title: Babe Ruth and the Home Run
body: Before 1920 baseball was a game of bunts, singles and stolen bases. After joining the New York Yankees in 1920, Babe Ruth hit home runs in numbers never seen before, including 60 in the 1927 season. His power hitting, helped by a livelier ball, transformed the sport and helped restore its popularity after the 1919 'Black Sox' betting scandal.

title: Go, the ancient game of territory
body: Go, known as weiqi in China and baduk in Korea, is a board game in which two players place black and white stones on a 19-by-19 grid to surround territory. It originated in China and has been played for well over 2,000 years. In Japan the Tokugawa shogunate supported professional Go houses from the 17th century, laying the foundations of the modern professional game.

title: Kathrine Switzer and the Boston Marathon
body: In 1967 Kathrine Switzer entered the men-only Boston Marathon as 'K. V. Switzer' and became the first woman to run it with an official race number. A race official tried to tear the number off her during the race, and photographs of the incident spread worldwide. Women were officially admitted in 1972, and a women's marathon entered the Olympics in 1984.

title: W. G. Grace and Victorian Cricket
body: William Gilbert Grace, a doctor from Gloucestershire, played first-class cricket from the 1860s until 1908. His batting, which combined forward and back play, shaped how the game was played, and his fame helped make cricket England's national summer game. Bearded and larger than life, he was one of the first true sporting celebrities.

title: The First Africa Cup of Nations
body: The Confederation of African Football was founded in 1957, and the first Africa Cup of Nations was held that year in Khartoum, Sudan, with only Egypt, Sudan and Ethiopia taking part. South Africa had been due to play but was excluded after insisting on sending an all-white team. Egypt won, and the tournament grew alongside decolonisation into a showcase for independent African nations.

title: Snooker's Indian Origins
body: Snooker is generally said to have been devised in the 1870s by British army officers in India, who added coloured balls to games on the billiard table; Jabalpur and Ooty are both linked to its origin. Its name came from army slang for a first-year cadet. The game spread to Britain and became a major televised sport in the colour television era.

title: Alice Milliat and the Women's World Games
body: When the International Olympic Committee refused to include women's track and field, the French sports organiser Alice Milliat set up an international women's sports federation in 1921 and held the first Women's World Games in Paris in 1922. Their success pressured the IOC, which added a small women's athletics programme at the 1928 Amsterdam Olympics. Milliat is remembered as a pioneer of women's international sport.

title: Black Jockeys and the Kentucky Derby
body: When the Kentucky Derby was first run in 1875, most of its riders were African American, including the winner, Oliver Lewis. Black jockeys such as Isaac Murphy, who won the Derby three times, were among the best-paid sportsmen of their era. By the early 20th century, segregation and discrimination had pushed them almost entirely out of the sport.

title: Laamb, Senegalese Wrestling
body: Laamb, Senegalese wrestling, grew out of village contests held after the harvest and is one of the country's most popular sports. Major bouts fill stadiums and combine wrestling with drumming, dance and protective rituals involving charms and mystical preparation. The modern version allows punches, which sets it apart from many other wrestling traditions.

title: The Football War
body: In 1969 El Salvador and Honduras fought a brief war soon after a bitter series of World Cup qualifying matches between them. The real causes were land disputes and the expulsion of Salvadoran migrants from Honduras, but violence around the games inflamed tensions. The conflict lasted about 100 hours; estimates of the dead vary widely, but most were civilians.

title: Nadia Comăneci's Perfect Ten
body: At the 1976 Montreal Olympics the 14-year-old Romanian gymnast Nadia Comăneci received the first perfect score of 10 in Olympic gymnastics, on the uneven bars. The scoreboard had not been built to show 10.00 and displayed '1.00' instead. She won three gold medals at those Games, and her performances helped make gymnastics a global television attraction.

title: Rugby's Great Split of 1895
body: In 1895 clubs in northern England broke away from the Rugby Football Union over 'broken-time' payments, compensation for working men who lost wages in order to play. They formed the Northern Union, whose game gradually changed its rules and became rugby league. Rugby union stayed officially amateur until 1995, a century later, so the split was as much about class as about sport.

title: Basketball's Dream Team
body: Olympic basketball long excluded professionals, which kept American NBA players out. After a rule change in 1989, the United States sent a team of NBA stars, including Michael Jordan, Magic Johnson and Larry Bird, to the 1992 Barcelona Olympics, where they won every game by wide margins. The 'Dream Team' spread the game's popularity around the world, and many more foreign players went on to join the NBA.

title: Hurling and the Gaelic Athletic Association
body: Hurling, played with a wooden stick called a hurley and a small ball, has ancient roots, with references in early medieval Irish law tracts and in legend. In 1884 the Gaelic Athletic Association was founded to preserve Irish games such as hurling and Gaelic football against English sports. The GAA became a pillar of Irish nationalism, and its players, who represent their home parish and county, have stayed amateur.

title: The Far Eastern Championship Games
body: In 1913 Manila hosted the first Far Eastern Championship Games, with teams from the Philippines, China and Japan. Encouraged by American YMCA organisers, they were among the first international multi-sport events in Asia and were held regularly until 1934. They paved the way for the later Asian Games.

title: The Webb Ellis Legend
body: Rugby's origin story says that in 1823 William Webb Ellis, a pupil at Rugby School, picked up the ball during a football match and ran with it. The story rests solely on the antiquarian Matthew Bloxam, who first wrote of it in 1876, more than 50 years after the supposed event and after Webb Ellis had died, and historians regard the tale as unproven. Even so, the Rugby World Cup trophy bears his name.

title: Iran versus the United States, 1998
body: At the 1998 World Cup in France, Iran and the United States, which had had no diplomatic relations since 1980, were drawn to play each other. Before kick-off the Iranian players presented their opponents with white roses, and the two teams posed together for a joint photograph. Iran won 2-1, prompting street celebrations at home, and the match was hailed as a moment of sporting goodwill.

title: The Myth of Abner Doubleday
body: In 1907 a commission set up by baseball's establishment declared that the Civil War officer Abner Doubleday had invented the game in Cooperstown, New York, in 1839. Historians have found no evidence for this: baseball evolved gradually from English bat-and-ball games such as rounders, and early rules were written down by New York clubs in the 1840s. The myth suited a wish to present baseball as purely American, and the Hall of Fame was later built in Cooperstown.

title: Bodyline
body: In the 1932-33 Ashes series in Australia, the England captain Douglas Jardine had his fast bowlers aim short-pitched balls at batsmen's bodies, with fielders packed on the leg side. The tactic, dubbed 'Bodyline', was designed to contain the great batsman Don Bradman. The bitter dispute strained relations between Australia and Britain and led cricket's lawmakers to restrict such bowling.

title: Wrestlers on the Tombs of Beni Hasan
body: Tombs at Beni Hasan in Middle Egypt, dating from around 2000 BC, are painted with hundreds of pairs of wrestlers showing a wide range of holds and throws. Together with other Egyptian images of sport, they are among the earliest detailed depictions of organised physical contests. They show that wrestling was a practised and taught skill more than a thousand years before the first recorded Greek Olympics.

title: Gertrude Ederle Swims the Channel
body: In 1926 the American swimmer Gertrude Ederle became the first woman to swim the English Channel, crossing from France to England. Her time of about 14 and a half hours was faster than that of any of the men who had made the crossing before her. Welcomed home with a ticker-tape parade in New York, she became a symbol of women's physical capability.

title: The World Nomad Games
body: First held in Kyrgyzstan in 2014, the World Nomad Games bring together traditional sports of Central Asian and other nomadic peoples. Events include horseback games, wrestling, archery and hunting with eagles. The Games were created to revive and celebrate a nomadic heritage that had been marginalised during the Soviet era.

title: Chariot Racing and the Nika Riots
body: Chariot racing was the great spectator sport of Rome and Byzantium, staged in vast arenas such as the Circus Maximus. Fans backed rival factions known by their colours, chiefly the Blues and the Greens, which also acted as political groupings. In 532 supporters of both rose together against Emperor Justinian in Constantinople; the Nika riots burned much of the city and were crushed with the deaths of many thousands.

title: Duke Kahanamoku and Surfing
body: Surfing was part of Polynesian culture for centuries, and in Hawaii it had religious and social meaning, with chiefs riding the longest boards. Discouraged by missionaries in the 19th century, it was revived in the early 20th century, notably by the Hawaiian swimmer Duke Kahanamoku, who won Olympic gold in 1912. His demonstrations in Australia in 1914-15 and in California helped spread surfing around the world.

title: Sepak Takraw
body: Sepak takraw is a Southeast Asian game in which players use their feet, knees, chest and head, but not their hands, to send a ball over a net. It grew from older games of keeping a woven rattan ball in the air, played across the region under different names. Southeast Asian officials, including from Malaysia and Thailand, agreed standard rules around 1960, and it became an Asian Games sport in 1990.

title: Babe Didrikson Zaharias
body: Mildred 'Babe' Didrikson won two gold medals and a silver in athletics at the 1932 Los Angeles Olympics, then turned to golf. She became one of the leading women golfers of the 1940s and 1950s and was a founding member of the Ladies Professional Golf Association in 1950. Her success across many sports challenged ideas of what women athletes could do.

title: Chaturanga and the Origins of Chess
body: Chess is generally traced to chaturanga, a game played in India by around the 6th century AD, whose pieces represented the four divisions of an army: infantry, cavalry, elephants and chariots. It passed to Persia as shatranj and spread through the Islamic world to Europe by around 1000. The word 'checkmate', from the Persian shah mat, recalls this journey.

title: The Maracanazo
body: Brazil hosted the 1950 World Cup and built the Maracanã stadium in Rio de Janeiro for it. In the deciding match Brazil needed only a draw, but Uruguay came from behind to win 2-1 before an official crowd of about 174,000, and perhaps over 200,000. The defeat, known as the Maracanazo, was felt as a national trauma, and Brazil soon abandoned its white kit for the yellow shirts that became its trademark.

title: Jousting and the Death of Henry II
body: Tournaments began in the Middle Ages as mock battles that trained knights for war, and later became courtly spectacles centred on the joust. In 1559 King Henry II of France was fatally wounded when a splintered lance pierced his eye during a joust in Paris. His death helped turn the French court away from jousting, which declined across Europe in the following decades.

title: Cuba's Amateur Sporting Model
body: After the 1959 revolution, Cuba abolished professional sport in the early 1960s and built a state system of sports schools and amateur athletes. The island became a major Olympic power, especially in boxing and baseball. The heavyweight Teófilo Stevenson won Olympic gold in 1972, 1976 and 1980 and famously turned down large offers to become a professional.

title: The First Modern Olympics
body: The French educator Pierre de Coubertin founded the International Olympic Committee in 1894 to revive the ancient Games as an international festival. The first modern Olympics were held in Athens in 1896 with only a few hundred male athletes. Their highlight was the new marathon race, won by the Greek water carrier Spyridon Louis, who became a national hero.

title: Archery in Bhutan
body: Archery is Bhutan's national sport and a central part of village and festival life. Teams shoot at small targets placed more than 100 metres apart, while teammates and spectators sing, dance and taunt their opponents. Matches are social occasions with food and drink, and traditional bamboo bows are used alongside modern ones.

title: Indonesia's First Olympic Gold
body: Badminton became a full Olympic sport at Barcelona in 1992, and Indonesia's Susi Susanti and Alan Budikusuma both won singles gold. They were Indonesia's first Olympic gold medals. The pair, who later married, were welcomed home with a parade, reflecting badminton's deep popularity in Indonesia.

title: Lucha Libre
body: Lucha libre, Mexican professional wrestling, became a mass spectacle from the 1930s, known for acrobatic moves and colourful masks. Losing one's mask in a bout is a great dishonour, and some wrestlers kept their identities secret for life. The masked wrestler El Santo became a folk hero and starred in dozens of films, making lucha libre part of Mexican popular culture.

title: Cuju, Ancient Chinese Football
body: Cuju, meaning 'kick ball', was a Chinese game in which players kicked a stuffed leather ball, recorded more than 2,000 years ago in the Warring States and Han periods. It was used in military training and later became a popular pastime, played with a raised goal net during the Song dynasty. FIFA has cited cuju as one of the earliest forms of football for which there is historical evidence.

title: Cold War Olympic Boycotts
body: In 1980 the United States led a boycott of the Moscow Olympics in protest at the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, and dozens of countries stayed away. The Soviet Union and most of its allies retaliated by boycotting the 1984 Los Angeles Games, citing security concerns. The tit-for-tat boycotts showed how fully the Olympics had become an arena of superpower rivalry.

title: Li Na's Grand Slam Breakthrough
body: In 2011 Li Na won the French Open, becoming the first player from Asia to win a Grand Slam singles title. She had broken away from China's state sports system to manage her own career and earnings. Her success sparked a surge of interest in tennis in China, and she added the Australian Open in 2014 before retiring that year.

title: Pakistan's Squash Dynasty
body: In 1951 Hashim Khan, a former squash court attendant from near Peshawar, won the British Open, then the sport's most important tournament, and went on to win it several more times. He and relatives from the same Pashtun community dominated the game for years, and later Pakistani players, including Jahangir Khan and Jansher Khan, led the sport in the 1980s and 1990s. Squash became a source of national pride for Pakistan.

title: Major Taylor, Cycling's Black Champion
body: Marshall 'Major' Taylor, an African American cyclist, won the world sprint championship in 1899, becoming the first African American world champion and only the second Black world champion in any sport. Cycle racing was then hugely popular, but he faced exclusion from races, threats and physical attacks from rivals. He raced with great success in Europe and Australia, where crowds celebrated him.

title: Kırkpınar Oil Wrestling
body: At Kırkpınar, near Edirne in Turkey, wrestlers coated in olive oil compete in an annual tournament whose tradition is said to go back to the 14th century, making it one of the oldest continuously held sporting events. Wrestlers wear heavy leather trousers and try to grip and pin opponents, which the oil makes very difficult. The champion wins the title of başpehlivan, or chief wrestler.

title: Asia's First World Cup
body: In 2002 Japan and South Korea jointly hosted the first FIFA World Cup in Asia, and the first shared by two countries. South Korea became the first Asian team to reach the semi-finals, amid mass street celebrations. Co-hosting between two countries with a difficult colonial history was itself seen as a diplomatic event.

title: The First Winter Olympics
body: In 1924 Chamonix in the French Alps hosted an 'International Winter Sports Week', later recognised as the first Winter Olympic Games. Events included cross-country skiing, ski jumping, skating, ice hockey and bobsleigh, and Nordic nations dominated. Figure skating and ice hockey had earlier appeared at Summer Games, but Chamonix established winter sports as a separate Olympic festival.

title: Capoeira
body: Capoeira is a Brazilian practice combining fighting, acrobatics, music and dance, developed by enslaved Africans and their descendants. It was repressed and outlawed in Brazil from 1890, but gained acceptance in the 1930s when masters such as Mestre Bimba opened academies. UNESCO recognised the capoeira circle as intangible cultural heritage in 2014.

title: Fischer versus Spassky, 1972
body: In 1972 the American Bobby Fischer played the Soviet champion Boris Spassky for the world chess title in Reykjavík, Iceland. Soviet players had held the title since 1948, and the match became a symbol of the Cold War. Fischer won, but he never defended his title and forfeited it in 1975.

title: Lacrosse, the Creator's Game
body: Lacrosse grew out of stick-and-ball games played by many Indigenous nations of eastern North America, including the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois), who call it the Creator's Game. Traditional matches could involve hundreds of players over long distances and had spiritual and diplomatic purposes. Canadians codified modern rules in the 1860s, and Haudenosaunee teams have competed internationally under their own flag.

title: Fanny Blankers-Koen, the Flying Housewife
body: At the 1948 London Olympics the Dutch sprinter Fanny Blankers-Koen, a 30-year-old mother of two, won four gold medals: the 100 m, 200 m, 80 m hurdles and 4 x 100 m relay. Critics had told her she was too old and should stay at home with her children. Nicknamed 'the Flying Housewife', she challenged assumptions about women, motherhood and athletic performance.

title: Video Replay Enters Sport
body: Television replays had long exposed officials' mistakes, but sports were slow to let technology overrule them. Tennis adopted the Hawk-Eye ball-tracking system for line calls in 2006, cricket introduced a player review system around 2008, and football used goal-line technology at the 2014 World Cup and video assistant referees at the 2018 World Cup. These changes reshaped debates about fairness, human judgement and the flow of play.

title: The All Blacks and the Haka
body: New Zealand's national rugby team toured Britain in 1905 and lost only one match, a tour on which the name All Blacks took hold and which made rugby central to the young nation's identity. The team performed a haka, a Māori ceremonial dance, before matches. The best-known haka, Ka Mate, is attributed to the Ngāti Toa chief Te Rauparaha in the early 19th century.

title: St Andrews and the Eighteen-Hole Round
body: Golf developed in eastern Scotland in the 15th century, played over the natural links land between town and sea. At St Andrews the Old Course was reduced from 22 holes to 18 in 1764, and this became the standard length of a round as the game spread. The Royal and Ancient Golf Club of St Andrews later became one of the sport's main rule-making bodies.

title: Abebe Bikila Runs Barefoot in Rome
body: At the 1960 Rome Olympics the Ethiopian soldier Abebe Bikila won the marathon running barefoot, finishing by the Arch of Constantine at night. He is widely regarded as the first Black African Olympic champion, and his victory in the capital of Italy, which had invaded Ethiopia in 1935, carried symbolic weight. In Tokyo in 1964 he became the first person to win the Olympic marathon twice.

title: The Football Association's Rules of 1863
body: In 1863 representatives of London clubs and schools met in a tavern to form the Football Association and agree common rules. They split over whether to allow carrying the ball and hacking, or kicking opponents' shins; clubs favouring those practices left, and their game developed into rugby. The FA's code became association football, shortened to 'soccer', which spread around the world.

title: The Battle of the Sexes
body: In 1973 the former men's champion Bobby Riggs, then 55, claimed that women's tennis was inferior and challenged leading female players. Billie Jean King beat him in straight sets in Houston before a vast television audience. The same year she led the founding of the Women's Tennis Association, and the US Open became the first major tournament to offer equal prize money to men and women.

title: Robot Jockeys in Camel Racing
body: Camel racing is a traditional sport of the Arabian Peninsula, where small children, often trafficked from South Asia and Africa, were long used as jockeys. After international criticism, Gulf states including the United Arab Emirates and Qatar banned child jockeys in the early 2000s. Light remote-controlled robot jockeys, steered by owners driving alongside the track, replaced them.

title: Kerry Packer's World Series Cricket
body: In 1977 the Australian media owner Kerry Packer, refused television rights to Test cricket, signed dozens of leading players for his own rival competition. World Series Cricket introduced coloured clothing, floodlit night matches, white balls and new styles of television coverage. The split ended in 1979 with a deal giving Packer's network the broadcasting rights, and it permanently commercialised the game.

title: Africa's First World Cup
body: In 2010 South Africa became the first African country to host the FIFA World Cup, sixteen years after its first democratic elections. The tournament brought new stadiums and transport links, though critics questioned the cost and the later use of some venues. It was widely seen as a symbolic moment for the continent and for post-apartheid South Africa.

title: Taekwondo
body: Taekwondo developed in South Korea in the 1940s and 1950s, as martial arts schools combined Korean traditions with influences from Japanese karate; the name was adopted in the mid-1950s. It is known for high, fast kicks. Promoted by the state as a national sport, it became a full Olympic event at Sydney in 2000.

title: Pehlwani, the Wrestling of the Akhara
body: Pehlwani is the traditional wrestling of the Indian subcontinent, practised in akharas, earthen training pits where wrestlers follow a strict regime of exercise, diet and celibacy. It blends Persian and older Indian traditions and is often devoted to the god Hanuman. Its most famous champion, the Great Gama, was celebrated in the early 20th century for a reputedly unbeaten career.

title: The 1964 Tokyo Olympics
body: The 1964 Tokyo Games were the first Olympics held in Asia, and Japan used them to present its recovery from war and defeat. The final torchbearer, Yoshinori Sakai, had been born near Hiroshima on the day the atomic bomb fell. The Shinkansen high-speed railway opened just before the Games, which were also the first to be broadcast live overseas by satellite.

title: The Indian Premier League
body: Launched in 2008, the Indian Premier League applied the short Twenty20 format to city-based franchises owned by businesses and celebrities, with players bought at auction. It brought international stars together in club teams for a few weeks each year and generated enormous broadcasting revenues. Its success inspired similar leagues around the world and shifted cricket's balance between national teams and franchise competitions.

title: The Rumble in the Jungle
body: In 1974 Muhammad Ali fought the heavyweight champion George Foreman in Kinshasa, Zaire, in a bout funded by President Mobutu's government. Ali absorbed Foreman's punches while leaning on the ropes, a tactic he called 'rope-a-dope', before knocking him out in the eighth round to regain the title. Promoted as a celebration of Black and African identity, it became one of the most famous sporting events of the century.

title: The Zurkhaneh, Iran's House of Strength
body: The zurkhaneh, or 'house of strength', is a traditional Iranian gymnasium where men exercise with heavy wooden clubs, shields and chains in a sunken octagonal pit. A master called the morshed sets the rhythm with a drum and recites poetry, including passages from Ferdowsi's Shahnameh. The practice blends athletics with ethics and spirituality, and UNESCO listed it as intangible cultural heritage in 2010.

title: Ludwig Guttmann and the Paralympic Movement
body: Ludwig Guttmann, a German-Jewish neurologist who had fled to Britain, used sport to rehabilitate patients with spinal injuries at Stoke Mandeville Hospital. On the opening day of the 1948 London Olympics he staged an archery contest for wheelchair athletes, which grew into the annual Stoke Mandeville Games. An international version held in Rome in 1960 is counted as the first Paralympic Games.

title: Buzkashi
body: Buzkashi, meaning 'goat grabbing', is a horseback game played across Central Asia and especially in Afghanistan, in which riders fight to seize a goat or calf carcass and carry it to a goal. Games can involve dozens of riders, and the most skilled horsemen, known in Afghanistan as chapandaz, are widely admired. Wealthy patrons have long sponsored riders and horses, and the game has carried prestige and political meaning.

title: The Birth of the Copa América
body: In 1916 Argentina hosted a South American football championship to mark the centenary of its independence, with Uruguay, Brazil and Chile taking part. The same year CONMEBOL, the South American football confederation, was founded, the first continental football body. The championship, later renamed the Copa América, is the oldest continental football competition still held.

title: Fiji's Olympic Sevens Gold
body: Rugby sevens entered the Olympics at the 2016 Rio Games, and Fiji won the men's tournament, beating Great Britain in the final. It was Fiji's first Olympic medal of any colour. Rugby is central to Fijian national life, and the victory was marked with a public holiday and a commemorative banknote.

title: The Munich Massacre
body: During the 1972 Munich Olympics, members of the Palestinian group Black September broke into the Olympic village and took members of the Israeli team hostage. Eleven Israeli athletes, coaches and officials were killed, along with a West German police officer, after a failed rescue at an airfield. The Games continued after a memorial service, and the attack transformed security at major sporting events.

title: Muay Thai, the Art of Eight Limbs
body: Muay Thai, or Thai boxing, is called 'the art of eight limbs' because fighters strike with fists, elbows, knees and shins. It developed from older Siamese combat traditions and became a ring sport with gloves and timed rounds in the 20th century. Bouts begin with the wai kru ram muay, a ritual dance paying respect to teachers, accompanied by live music.

title: The World Anti-Doping Agency
body: In 1998 French customs officers found large quantities of banned drugs, including the blood-boosting hormone EPO, in a Festina team car before the Tour de France, exposing systematic doping in professional cycling. The scandal prompted the International Olympic Committee to call a conference that led to the founding of the World Anti-Doping Agency in 1999. WADA introduced a single code of banned substances and testing rules across sports and countries.

title: West Indies Cricket and Independence
body: In 1960 Frank Worrell became the first Black cricketer appointed to captain the West Indies for a full series, after a campaign supported by the Trinidadian writer C. L. R. James. His team's tour of Australia in 1960-61 was celebrated for its spirit and skill as Caribbean colonies moved towards independence. James's book Beyond a Boundary (1963) presented cricket as a lens on race, class and colonialism.

title: The FA's Ban on Women's Football
body: During and after the First World War, women's football drew huge crowds in Britain; a 1920 Boxing Day match involving Dick, Kerr Ladies attracted over 50,000 spectators. In 1921 the Football Association banned women's teams from its members' grounds, calling the game 'quite unsuitable for females'. The ban lasted 50 years, until 1971, and held back the women's game for generations.

title: Sohn Kee-chung's Marathon
body: The 1936 Olympic marathon was won by Sohn Kee-chung, a Korean forced to compete for Japan, which then ruled Korea. On the podium he bowed his head as the Japanese anthem played. A Korean newspaper that printed his photograph with the Japanese flag erased from his shirt was suspended by the colonial authorities, and Sohn is honoured in Korea as a national hero.

title: American Football's Crisis of 1905
body: Early American college football was so violent that players were killed every season. In 1905 President Theodore Roosevelt summoned college leaders to the White House to demand reform, and a new rules body was formed that later became the NCAA. The reforms legalised the forward pass from 1906, gradually turning a game of mass scrimmages into a passing game.

title: The First Women Olympic Champions
body: Women first competed at the Olympics in Paris in 1900, in a handful of sports such as tennis, golf and sailing. The British tennis player Charlotte Cooper became the first woman to win an individual Olympic title. The founder of the modern Games, Pierre de Coubertin, opposed women's participation, and they were admitted to more events only gradually over the following decades.

title: Muhammad Ali Refuses the Draft
body: In 1967 the heavyweight champion Muhammad Ali refused induction into the US Army, citing his Muslim faith and opposition to the Vietnam War. He was stripped of his title and barred from boxing for more than three years in his prime. In 1971 the Supreme Court overturned his conviction, and his stand made him a worldwide symbol of protest.

title: Kip Keino and East African Running
body: At the 1968 Mexico City Olympics the Kenyan runner Kipchoge Keino won the 1,500 m by a wide margin over the American favourite Jim Ryun, despite suffering severe abdominal pains, later attributed to gallbladder problems. His victory, together with other Kenyan and Ethiopian medals at those high-altitude Games, announced East Africa as a power in distance running. Keino later devoted himself to caring for orphaned children in Kenya.

title: The Bosman Ruling
body: In 1995 the European Court of Justice ruled in favour of the Belgian footballer Jean-Marc Bosman, whose club had blocked his transfer after his contract expired. Players in the European Union became free to move when their contracts ended, and limits on players from other EU countries were struck down. The ruling shifted power and money from clubs to players and made European club squads far more international.

title: Koshien and Japanese Baseball
body: Baseball was introduced to Japan in the 1870s by the American teacher Horace Wilson and became one of the country's most popular sports. The national high school tournament, first held in 1915 and played at Koshien Stadium since 1924, draws huge national audiences each summer. Japanese baseball developed its own culture emphasising discipline, teamwork and relentless practice.

title: India's 1983 Cricket World Cup
body: India, little regarded in one-day cricket, beat the two-time champions West Indies in the 1983 World Cup final at Lord's under the captaincy of Kapil Dev. The victory turned limited-overs cricket into a national passion. Over the following decades India's vast audience and television market made it the financial centre of world cricket.

title: The Sporting Boycott of Apartheid
body: South Africa's apartheid policies led to its exclusion from the Olympics from 1964, and it was expelled from the Olympic movement in 1970. In 1968 the government refused to accept an England cricket touring team that included Basil D'Oliveira, a mixed-race player born in Cape Town, and the tour was cancelled. Sporting isolation, which lasted until the early 1990s, was one of the most visible international pressures on the apartheid regime.

title: Total Football
body: Total Football was a style developed in the Netherlands in the late 1960s and 1970s by the coach Rinus Michels at Ajax and with the national team, with Johan Cruyff as its leading player. Outfield players constantly swapped positions, so any of them could attack or defend while the team kept its shape. Its ideas of fluid movement, pressing and possession deeply influenced modern football tactics.

title: Jack Johnson and the 'Great White Hope'
body: In 1908 Jack Johnson became the first African American world heavyweight boxing champion. His victories and defiance of racial conventions provoked a search for a 'Great White Hope' to beat him, and his 1910 win over James Jeffries set off racist violence across the United States. His later conviction under a law on transporting women across state lines was widely seen as racially motivated, and he was posthumously pardoned in 2018.

title: The Tour de France
body: The Tour de France was created in 1903 by the sports newspaper L'Auto to boost its sales against a rival paper. Its editor Henri Desgrange set gruelling stages, and the race became a national ritual passing through towns and villages across France. The leader's yellow jersey, introduced in 1919, matched the colour of the paper on which L'Auto was printed.

title: The 1968 Mexico City Olympics
body: The 1968 Mexico City Games were the first Olympics held in Latin America. Days before they opened, security forces killed many student protesters at Tlatelolco in the capital. The thin air at about 2,240 metres helped Bob Beamon's long jump of 8.90 metres, and on the podium the American sprinters Tommie Smith and John Carlos raised gloved fists in protest against racial injustice.

title: The Founding of FIFA
body: FIFA was founded in Paris in 1904 by representatives of seven European national football associations; England's FA, at first sceptical, joined in 1905. It set out to govern the game internationally and later created the World Cup. Its membership grew rapidly with decolonisation, as newly independent states joined and made football a truly global sport.

title: Jim Thorpe and the Amateur Rules
body: At the 1912 Stockholm Olympics Jim Thorpe, a member of the Sac and Fox Nation, won both the pentathlon and the decathlon. His medals were taken away in 1913 because he had been paid for playing minor-league baseball, breaking the strict amateur rules of the time. He went on to play professional baseball and American football, and his Olympic titles were restored long after his death.
